specStatements.text: The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time:
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken)
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken)
The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s.
For the Higher Tier, students are also required to use quantity of reactants in terms of moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s.
Students should be able to:
calculate the mean rate of a reaction from given information about the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of a product formed and the time taken
draw, and interpret, graphs showing the quantity of product formed or quantity of reactant used up against time
draw tangents to the curves on these graphs and use the slope of the tangent as a measure of the rate of reaction
(HT only) calculate the gradient of a tangent to the curve on these graphs as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.

Factors which affect the rates of chemical reactions include: the concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
Students should be able to recall how changing these factors affects the rate of chemical reactions.

Required practical 5: investigate how changes in concentration affect the rates of reactions by a method involving measuring the volume of a gas produced and a method involving a change in colour or turbidity.
This should be an investigation involving developing a hypothesis.

Collision theory explains how various factors affect rates of reactions. According to this theory, chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.

Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, and the surface area of solid reactants increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.
Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.
Students should be able to :
predict and explain using collision theory the effects of changing conditions of concentration, pressure and temperature on the rate of a reaction
predict and explain the effects of changes in the size of pieces of a reacting solid in terms of surface area to volume ratio
use simple ideas about proportionality when using collision theory to explain the effect of a factor on the rate of a reaction.
Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.
A reaction profile for a catalysed reaction can be drawn in the following form:
Students should be able to identify catalysts in reactions from their effect on the rate of reaction and because they are not included in the chemical equation for the reaction.
Students should be able to explain catalytic action in terms of activation energy.
Students do not need to know the names of catalysts other than those specified in the subject content.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of catalysts other than those specified in the subject content.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks a student to recall the name of a catalyst. Where a named substance appears (manganese(IV) oxide in q33, the unnamed solid in q34), the name is supplied in the stem as data and the question tests the skill the specification does require: identifying a catalyst from its effect on the rate and from its absence from the chemical equation. Enzymes are named only because the specification itself names them as biological catalysts. No item requires catalysts for industrial processes, transition-metal catalyst names, or the substance-specific catalysts met elsewhere in the course, and no item asks for a catalyst to be matched to a named reaction from memory.

scopeNotes.statement: For the Higher Tier, students are also required to use quantity of reactants in terms of moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s. (HT only) calculate the gradient of a tangent to the curve on these graphs as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two requirements the specification restricts to the Higher Tier are kept inside items tagged tier "higher" and nowhere else. Moles as a quantity of reactant and mol/s as a unit of rate appear only in c07, m10, q06 and q07. Numerical calculation of the gradient of a tangent appears only in c13, q14 and q15. Foundation-accessible items use only mass in grams and volume in cm³, and ask only for a tangent to be drawn and its steepness compared (q12, q13), which is what the specification requires of both tiers. The input file records the tier of the moles statement as "both" and that value is copied verbatim in specStatements; the items derived from it are tagged "higher" because the statement's own wording restricts the requirement to the Higher Tier.

concepts.definition: How quickly a reaction proceeds. The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.

A single measurement cannot give a rate. The quantity of reactant used, or of product formed, has to be recorded together with the time over which that change happened, so that one can be divided by the other.
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken). The quantity of reactant used is the difference between the starting quantity and the quantity left, not the quantity left itself.
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken). Both forms give a mean, that is, an average over the whole period timed, not the rate at any one instant within it.

The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³. Mass is used when a solid is consumed or a gas escapes from an open flask; volume is used when a gas is collected, for example in a gas syringe.
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³/s. The unit always carries a quantity divided by a time; a quantity on its own, such as 25 cm³, is not a rate.

For the Higher Tier, the quantity of reactants may also be expressed in moles, and the rate of reaction then has the units mol/s. The calculation is unchanged: moles used or formed, divided by the time taken.

concepts.term: Graph of product formed against time
concepts.definition: A graph of the quantity of product formed against time starts steep and becomes less steep, finally levelling off. The steep early part shows the fastest rate; the flattening shows the reaction slowing.

When the line on the graph becomes horizontal, no more product is being formed: the reaction has finished because one of the reactants has been completely used up. The height of the horizontal section gives the total quantity of product formed.

A graph of the quantity of a reactant used up against time rises and then levels off, in the same way as a product graph. If instead the quantity of reactant remaining is plotted, the line falls steeply at first and then levels off.
A straight line drawn so that it just touches a curve at one chosen point, matching the steepness of the curve at that point. It is drawn to measure the rate at that moment rather than the mean rate.

concepts.term: Slope as a measure of rate
concepts.definition: The slope of the tangent is used as a measure of the rate of reaction at that time. A steeper tangent means a faster reaction; as the curve flattens the tangents become less steep, showing the rate falling.

The gradient of the tangent is calculated as the change in the quantity plotted on the vertical axis divided by the change in time along the horizontal axis, taken between two well-separated points on the tangent. It gives the rate of reaction at that specific time.

Factors which affect the rates of chemical reactions include: the concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
How many particles of the dissolved reactant there are in a given volume of solution. Increasing the concentration increases the rate of reaction.
Increasing the pressure of reacting gases pushes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume, so they are closer together. Increasing the pressure increases the rate of reaction.
The area of solid that is exposed to the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces, or grinding it to a powder, increases the surface area and so increases the rate of reaction.
Increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction; decreasing it slows the reaction down. This is why cooling is used to slow unwanted reactions such as food spoiling.
Adding a suitable catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. The catalyst is a further factor that can be changed, alongside concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature.

One method of following a reaction is to collect the gas produced, for example hydrogen from magnesium and hydrochloric acid, and record the volume in the gas syringe at fixed time intervals. Repeating this at different acid concentrations shows how concentration affects the rate.

concepts.term: Colour change or turbidity method (Required practical 5)
concepts.definition: The second method follows a reaction that clouds the mixture, for example sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid, which forms a precipitate of sulfur. The time taken for a cross viewed through the flask to disappear is measured; a shorter time means a faster reaction.

A testable idea, based on some scientific reasoning, about how one variable will affect another. In this investigation the hypothesis links the concentration of the solution to the rate of reaction and gives a reason for the link, so that the experiment can then test it.

Collision theory explains how various factors affect rates of reactions. According to this theory, chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
A collision that leads to a reaction. Colliding is not enough on its own: the colliding particles must also have at least the activation energy, so many collisions do not result in a reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. Particles that collide with less than this energy simply bounce apart unchanged.

How often collisions between reacting particles happen. Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, and the surface area of solid reactants increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.

Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction. Temperature is the only one of these factors that changes both how often particles collide and how much energy they collide with.

The surface area of a piece of solid compared with its volume. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces leaves the total volume unchanged but increases the total surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio increases and the reaction is faster.

A simple proportional argument used to explain the size of an effect: doubling the concentration of a solution puts twice as many reactant particles into the same volume, so collisions are twice as frequent and the rate is roughly doubled.

A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts, so a catalyst for one reaction will not necessarily work for another.
A biological catalyst. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems, speeding up reactions in living things without being used up.

Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy. Because less energy is needed, a greater proportion of the collisions have enough energy to react, so the reaction is faster.

concepts.term: Reaction profile for a catalysed reaction
concepts.definition: A reaction profile for a catalysed reaction is drawn with two curves between the same reactant and product energy levels: the uncatalysed pathway with the higher peak, and the catalysed pathway with a lower peak. The lower peak shows the lower activation energy; the overall energy change is unaltered.

A catalyst can be identified from its effect on the rate of reaction and because it is not included in the chemical equation for the reaction. It is present at the end in the same amount as at the start.

misconceptions.question: Reaction A finishes in 20 s and reaction B takes 200 s. Which has the greater rate?
misconceptions.correct: Reaction A. A short time for the same amount of change means a high rate.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction that goes on for longer has the bigger rate, because a bigger number of seconds must mean more reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Time is the number the student measured, so it feels like the answer, and in everyday speech 'a long reaction' sounds like 'a big reaction'. The dividing step is skipped.
misconceptions.correction: Time is the denominator, not the rate. Mean rate of reaction = quantity of reactant used (or product formed) divided by the time taken, so a longer time gives a smaller rate for the same quantity.

misconceptions.question: A reaction produces 60 cm³ of gas. Is 60 cm³ the rate of the reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate is that volume divided by the time taken, for example 60 cm³ in 30 s gives 2 cm³/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The rate is just how much gas you collected, or how much reactant disappeared; the bigger the amount, the bigger the rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The quantity is the impressive, visible measurement, and questions often quote it first. Students treat 'how much' and 'how fast' as the same question.
misconceptions.correction: Rate always involves time. Mean rate of reaction = quantity of product formed / time taken, so the quantity on its own is only half of the calculation.

misconceptions.question: 18 cm³ of gas is collected in 60 s. Is the rate 60 / 18?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate is 18 / 60 = 0.3 cm³/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Rate is time divided by quantity, so you put the bigger number on top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who cannot recall which way round the formula goes divide the larger number by the smaller to avoid a decimal answer, and the resulting number looks tidier.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states mean rate of reaction = quantity / time taken. Checking the units settles it: cm³ divided by s gives cm³/s, which is a rate; s divided by cm³ is not.

misconceptions.question: The volume of gas collected keeps increasing as the reaction goes on. Is the reaction getting faster?
misconceptions.correct: No. The total volume keeps rising, but the rate is falling, shown by the curve becoming less steep.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction speeds up as it goes on, because the line on the graph keeps going up and the total keeps getting bigger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the height of the line instead of its steepness, and a rising line reads intuitively as 'increasing'.
misconceptions.correction: On these graphs the height shows how much has been made so far, while the steepness shows the rate. The reaction is fastest at the start, when the reactants are most concentrated, and slows as they are used up.

misconceptions.question: The mean rate over 100 s is 0.5 cm³/s. Is the rate at 20 s also 0.5 cm³/s?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate at 20 s is found from the slope of a tangent at 20 s, and is usually greater than the mean.
misconceptions.misconception: There is only one rate for a reaction, so the mean rate and the rate at a particular moment must be the same number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'rate' is used for both, and Foundation questions often ask only for a mean, so the distinction never comes up until a tangent is required.
misconceptions.correction: The mean rate averages the whole period, including the slow end. The rate at a specific time is measured by the slope of the tangent drawn at that point on the curve.

misconceptions.question: To find the rate at 40 s, can you draw a line from the origin to the point on the curve at 40 s?
misconceptions.correct: No. That line gives the mean rate up to 40 s. A tangent must touch the curve at 40 s.
misconceptions.misconception: A tangent is the straight line you draw from the start of the graph to the point you are interested in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both constructions are straight lines drawn onto a curve, and drawing from the origin is easier because there are two clear points to join.
misconceptions.correction: A tangent just touches the curve at the chosen point and runs alongside it there, crossing the curve nowhere else nearby. Its slope is the rate at that time.

misconceptions.question: Which part of the curve shows the faster reaction, the steep part or the flat part?
misconceptions.correct: The steep part. A steeper slope means a greater rate of reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: The flatter part shows the faster reaction, because the line is racing along the graph rather than climbing slowly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the picture of a distance-time graph or of a car on a flat road, where 'flat and fast' feels natural, instead of reading the vertical change per second.
misconceptions.correction: The slope of the tangent is used as a measure of the rate. A flat line means the quantity is not changing at all, so the rate there is zero.

misconceptions.question: Why does the graph level off at the end of the reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Because one of the reactants has been completely used up, so no more product can form.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles have run out of energy after all that colliding, or the mixture has cooled down, so the reaction gives up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Running out of energy' matches everyday experience of getting tired, and students know reactions slow as they cool, so they reach for that explanation instead of checking what has been consumed.
misconceptions.correction: Particles do not run out of energy; the reaction stops because there is nothing left to react. If more of the used-up reactant is added, the reaction starts again.

misconceptions.question: A student writes 'rate = 0.4 cm³'. What is wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The unit is incomplete. The units of rate may be given as g/s or cm³/s.
misconceptions.misconception: The unit of rate is just the unit of whatever you measured, so cm³ or g on its own is fine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The unit is copied from the measuring instrument, and the division by time is done on the calculator without changing what is written down.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing a volume in cm³ by a time in s gives a unit of cm³/s; dividing a mass in grams by a time gives g/s. Without the 'per second' the number is a quantity, not a rate.

misconceptions.question: 0.050 mol of gas forms in 25 s. Can the rate be given in mol/s?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. On the Higher Tier the quantity may be in moles and the rate in mol/s, here 0.0020 mol/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Rate must always be in g/s or cm³/s, so a quantity in moles has to be converted to a mass before a rate can be worked out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The units g/s and cm³/s are met first and are the ones printed in most Foundation questions, so mol/s looks like something that must be wrong.
misconceptions.correction: For the Higher Tier, students are also required to use quantity of reactants in terms of moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s. The calculation is the same: moles divided by time.

misconceptions.question: Why does more concentrated acid react faster with magnesium?
misconceptions.correct: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so collisions with the metal are more frequent.
misconceptions.misconception: Concentrated acid gives each of its particles more energy, so more of the collisions are successful.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Stronger' and 'more powerful' are used loosely for concentrated solutions, which suggests energy rather than crowding, and energy is the other half of collision theory the student has learned.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration changes how crowded the particles are, not how energetic they are. Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate.

misconceptions.question: Why does raising the pressure speed up a reaction between two gases?
misconceptions.correct: The particles are pushed closer together, so they collide more frequently.
misconceptions.misconception: Squeezing a gas makes its particles move faster, so they hit each other harder and react more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compressing a gas does warm it in everyday experience, such as a bicycle pump, so students merge pressure with temperature.
misconceptions.correction: At the same temperature the particles have the same average energy however tightly they are packed. Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.

misconceptions.question: Give the full reason why heating a mixture speeds up the reaction.
misconceptions.correct: The collisions become both more frequent and more energetic, so more of them are successful.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating makes the particles move faster so they collide more often, and that is the whole explanation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The frequency argument is used for concentration, pressure and surface area, so students apply the same single sentence to temperature and stop there.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction. Both parts are needed, and the energy part is the more important one.

misconceptions.question: Does heating change how often particles collide?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Faster-moving particles collide more frequently as well as more energetically.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature only affects the energy of the collisions; how often particles meet is fixed by how crowded they are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once a student learns that temperature is 'the energy factor', they treat frequency as belonging exclusively to concentration, pressure and surface area.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature does both. Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic.

misconceptions.question: Two reactant particles collide. Do they react?
misconceptions.correct: Only if they collide with at least the activation energy; otherwise they bounce apart unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Every collision between the right particles produces a reaction, so rate is simply about how often they meet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The frequency half of collision theory is easier to picture and is used to explain most factors, so the energy condition is quietly dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. Collisions below the activation energy achieve nothing.

misconceptions.question: What is the activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
misconceptions.misconception: The activation energy is the energy the reaction gives out once it gets going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are marked on a reaction profile, and 'activation' sounds like the burst of energy released when something is set off.
misconceptions.correction: Activation energy is the energy barrier that has to be reached before a reaction can happen. The energy given out or taken in overall is the separate quantity shown between the reactant and product levels.

misconceptions.question: 5 g of marble chips is ground to a powder. Is there now more solid to react?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is still 5 g; only the exposed surface area has increased.
misconceptions.misconception: Grinding a solid up makes more of it, which is why the powder reacts faster and fizzes more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A powder looks bulkier and spreads further than a lump, and the reaction is visibly more vigorous, which suggests there is more material.
misconceptions.correction: The mass and the number of particles are unchanged. Breaking the solid up exposes particles that were buried inside, increasing the surface area to volume ratio and so the frequency of collisions.

misconceptions.question: Why does powdered zinc react faster than a lump of zinc?
misconceptions.correct: The powder has a much greater surface area to volume ratio, so collisions with the acid are more frequent.
misconceptions.misconception: The powder grains are small and light, so they move about faster and hit the acid particles harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer particle motion, which belongs to gases and solutions, to lumps of solid, and small grains do get stirred about visibly in the liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Grains of a solid are not particles in the chemical sense and their movement is not the point. What matters is how much of the solid's surface the acid particles can reach.

misconceptions.question: Does heating a reaction, or making it more concentrated, lower its activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. The activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway; only a catalyst provides a pathway with a lower one.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that speeds a reaction up must be lowering the activation energy, since that is what makes reactions easier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Activation energy is introduced as the reason reactions are slow, so it becomes the all-purpose explanation for any change in rate.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration, pressure and surface area change the frequency of collisions; temperature changes frequency and energy. The activation energy itself is unchanged. Catalysts increase the rate by providing a different pathway that has a lower activation energy.

misconceptions.question: Is a catalyst used up during a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is slowly consumed as it does its work, so it has to be topped up or replaced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything added to a reaction is assumed to take part in it, and students know a catalyst must contact the reactants to have an effect.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst can be recovered at the end with its mass unchanged, and the same sample can be used again. It is not one of the reactants.

misconceptions.question: How does a catalyst make more collisions successful?
misconceptions.correct: It provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst gives the particles extra energy, pushing more of them over the activation energy barrier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that if more collisions now succeed, the particles must have been given more energy, since energy is the thing that decides success.
misconceptions.correction: The particles' energy is unchanged. The barrier is lowered instead, because the reaction now follows a different pathway, so the energy the particles already have is enough more often.

misconceptions.question: Does a catalyst change how much energy a reaction gives out overall?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the activation energy is lowered; the reactant and product energy levels are unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst lowers the whole profile, so the products end up lower and the reaction releases less energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Lower activation energy' is remembered simply as 'lower', and on the profile the catalysed curve is drawn lower at the peak, which is read as lower everywhere.
misconceptions.correction: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, both curves start and finish at the same levels. Only the height of the peak differs, because only the activation energy changes.

misconceptions.question: Does adding a catalyst increase the amount of product formed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The same quantity of product forms, it just forms sooner.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst makes the reaction produce more product, because a faster reaction gets more done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: On a graph the catalysed curve rises far more steeply, and students read the early lead as a bigger final total rather than checking where the two lines level off.
misconceptions.correction: Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions. The final amount of product is fixed by the quantity of reactants, so both curves level off at the same height.

misconceptions.question: A catalyst speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Will it speed up any reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Different reactions need different catalysts.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is a general speeding-up substance, so once you have one you can use it on anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition students memorise says only 'speeds up a reaction without being used up', which contains nothing to tie a catalyst to one particular reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Catalysts work by providing a different pathway for one particular reaction, so each reaction needs a catalyst suited to it.

misconceptions.question: Are enzymes catalysts?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
misconceptions.misconception: Enzymes are not really catalysts, because catalysts are chemicals used in industry and enzymes are made by living things.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Enzymes are met in biology and catalysts in chemistry, so the two are stored as separate topics with separate vocabulary.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They increase the rate of reactions in living systems and are not used up, exactly as any other catalyst.

misconceptions.question: Should a catalyst be written into the balanced equation as a reactant?
misconceptions.correct: No. Catalysts are not included in the chemical equation for the reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst has to go on the left of the arrow with the other things you put into the flask.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students build equations from what is physically added to the apparatus rather than from what is chemically changed.
misconceptions.correction: An equation shows the substances used up and formed. A catalyst is unchanged overall, so it does not appear; this is one way of identifying it.

misconceptions.question: The cross disappears in 25 s with one solution and 60 s with another. Which reaction was faster?
misconceptions.correct: The one taking 25 s. A shorter time to reach the same cloudiness means a faster reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: The 60 s reaction was faster, because it went on producing sulfur for much longer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stopwatch reading is the only number recorded, and a bigger number is instinctively read as 'more reaction' rather than 'more time needed'.
misconceptions.correction: The reaction is being timed to a fixed end point. The rate is proportional to 1 divided by the time, so the shorter the time, the greater the rate.

misconceptions.question: Is 'the cross disappeared faster with the concentrated solution' a hypothesis?
misconceptions.correct: No. That is the result. A hypothesis is proposed beforehand and gives a reason to be tested.
misconceptions.misconception: The hypothesis is what you found out at the end of the experiment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hypothesis, prediction and conclusion are all one-sentence statements about the same relationship, so students treat them as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: A hypothesis is developed before the investigation. It states the expected relationship and the scientific reason for it, so the experiment can test whether the reasoning holds.

misconceptions.question: Doubling the acid concentration doubles the rate. Does it also double the gas produced?
misconceptions.correct: No, if the magnesium is the reactant that runs out. The same volume of gas forms, just sooner.
misconceptions.misconception: More concentrated acid means more gas altogether, because there is more acid reacting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rate and yield are confused, and the steeper early curve looks as though it is heading for a higher final value.
misconceptions.correction: The final quantity of product is set by the reactant that is used up completely. Changing the concentration changes how quickly that point is reached, not where the graph levels off.

misconceptions.question: A cube is cut into eight smaller cubes. What happens to the surface area to volume ratio?
misconceptions.correct: It increases: the total volume is unchanged but the total surface area is greater.
misconceptions.misconception: Smaller pieces must have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, because everything about a small piece is smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Smaller' is applied to the ratio as if it were another dimension, without comparing the two quantities that make it up.
misconceptions.correction: Cutting exposes new faces that were previously inside the solid. The volume stays the same while the surface area rises, so the ratio rises, which is why powders react fastest.

misconceptions.question: Is 'I will change the concentration and keep the temperature the same' a hypothesis?
misconceptions.correct: No. That describes the variables. A hypothesis states the expected effect and the reason for it.
misconceptions.misconception: A hypothesis is the sentence where you say which variable you will change and which you will control.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Independent and control variables are drilled at the start of every practical write-up, so that sentence becomes the automatic answer to any planning question.
misconceptions.correction: Choosing variables is part of the method. The hypothesis is the testable idea itself, for example that a higher concentration gives more frequent collisions and therefore a greater rate.

misconceptions.question: The same mass of magnesium is used with acid of two different concentrations. Will the rates be the same?
misconceptions.correct: No. The more concentrated acid gives the greater rate, even though the mass of magnesium is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The rate depends on how much of the reactant that gets used up there is, so if the magnesium is the same the rate must be the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch on to the reactant that limits the total amount of product and assume it must control the speed as well.
misconceptions.correction: The limiting reactant fixes how much product forms; the conditions fix how fast it forms. Increasing the concentration of the acid increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate.

misconceptions.question: What is plotted along the bottom of a reaction profile?
misconceptions.correct: The progress of the reaction, from reactants to products. It is not a time axis.
misconceptions.misconception: The horizontal axis is time, so a catalysed reaction should be drawn as a shorter curve.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other graph in this topic has time along the bottom, so the axis is assumed to be the same one again.
misconceptions.correction: A reaction profile shows energy against the progress of the reaction. The catalysed pathway is drawn with a lower peak, not a shorter one; how fast the reaction goes is shown by the height of that barrier, not by the width of the diagram.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to find the rate of a reaction between marble chips and dilute acid, which gives off carbon dioxide. Which set of measurements would allow the rate to be found?

options.text: The volume of gas collected, recorded every 10 seconds
options.rationale: The rate can be found by measuring the quantity of product formed over time, so a quantity and a time are both needed.

options.text: The total volume of gas given off, and nothing else
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat 'how much' as the same question as 'how fast'; without a time this cannot give a rate.

options.text: The time until the fizzing stops, and nothing else
options.rationale: The stopwatch reading feels like the answer, but time alone is only the denominator of the calculation.

options.text: The temperature of the mixture, recorded every 10 seconds
options.rationale: Recorded over time, so it looks like the right shape of measurement, but temperature is not a quantity of reactant or product.

mcqs.stem: In a reaction, 3.6 g of magnesium ribbon is used up in 180 seconds. What is the mean rate of the reaction?

options.text: 50 g/s
options.rationale: 180 / 3.6, the formula inverted to avoid a decimal answer.
Mean rate = quantity of reactant used / time taken = 3.6 / 180 = 0.02 g/s.
The quantity quoted as if it were the rate, with the division by time omitted.
3.6 multiplied by 180; the student combines the two given numbers without thinking about what a rate is.

mcqs.stem: A gas syringe collects 54 cm³ of gas in 90 seconds. What is the mean rate of the reaction?

options.text: 1.7 cm³/s
options.rationale: 90 / 54, the formula the wrong way round, which conveniently gives an answer greater than 1.

options.text: 54 cm³
options.rationale: The measured volume repeated with the instrument's unit; no division and no 'per second'.

options.text: 0.6 cm³/s
options.rationale: Mean rate = quantity of product formed / time taken = 54 / 90 = 0.6 cm³/s.

options.text: 6.0 cm³/s
options.rationale: The correct division carried out but the decimal point misplaced by a factor of ten.

mcqs.stem: The specification states how the quantity of a reactant or product may be measured. Which pair of measurements does it give?

options.text: The mass in grams or the time taken in s
options.rationale: Time is offered as a measure of the quantity by students who have not separated the two parts of the formula.

options.text: The volume in cm³ divided by the time in s
options.rationale: This is the rate itself, not the quantity that goes into the rate calculation.

options.text: The temperature in °C or the volume in cm³
options.rationale: Temperature is a condition that affects the rate, not a quantity of reactant used or product formed.

options.text: The mass in grams or the volume in cm³
options.rationale: The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a unit of rate of reaction as given in the specification?

options.text: cm³/s
options.rationale: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³/s: a quantity divided by a time.

options.text: s/cm³
options.rationale: The inverted formula produces this unit, and it looks plausible to a student who divides time by volume.

options.text: cm³
options.rationale: The unit read straight off the gas syringe, with the 'per second' left off.

options.text: g/cm³
options.rationale: A density unit, chosen because it has the same two-part shape as a rate unit.

mcqs.stem: On the Higher Tier, the quantity of a reactant may be given in moles. Which unit is then used for the rate of reaction?

options.text: s/mol
options.rationale: Produced by dividing the time by the number of moles.

options.text: mol/s
options.rationale: Higher Tier students are required to use quantity of reactants in moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s.

options.text: mol
options.rationale: The quantity's own unit, kept unchanged because the division by time is not reflected in what is written.

options.text: g/s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe rate must always be reported in g/s, so the moles have to be converted to a mass first.

mcqs.stem: In a Higher Tier question, 0.060 mol of hydrogen is produced in 30 s. What is the mean rate of the reaction?

options.text: 500 mol/s
options.rationale: 30 / 0.060, the formula inverted, which turns a small decimal into a large whole number.

options.text: 0.060 mol/s
options.rationale: The quantity given a rate unit without being divided by the time.
Mean rate = quantity of product formed / time taken = 0.060 / 30 = 0.0020 mol/s.

options.text: 1.8 mol/s
options.rationale: 0.060 multiplied by 30, chosen because multiplying avoids the awkward small decimal.

mcqs.stem: A flask of reacting mixture stands on a balance. Its mass is 82.50 g at the start and 81.60 g after 60 s. What is the mean rate of the reaction?

options.rationale: The mass lost quoted as the rate, with the division by 60 s left out.
60 / 0.90, the formula the wrong way round.
81.60 / 60: the final mass used instead of the change in mass.
The mass lost is 82.50 − 81.60 = 0.90 g, so the mean rate is 0.90 / 60 = 0.015 g/s.

mcqs.stem: Experiment X produces 30 cm³ of gas in 20 s. Experiment Y produces 45 cm³ of gas in 45 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X has the greater mean rate, 1.5 cm³/s against 1.0 cm³/s
options.rationale: 30 / 20 = 1.5 cm³/s and 45 / 45 = 1.0 cm³/s, so X is the faster reaction.

options.text: Y has the greater mean rate, as it produced more gas in total
options.rationale: The larger volume is read as the larger rate, without dividing by the time.

options.text: Y has the greater mean rate, as it reacted for a longer time
options.rationale: A longer time is taken as evidence of a faster reaction rather than a slower one.

options.text: Both have the same mean rate, as the reactants were the same
options.rationale: Assumes the identity of the chemicals fixes the rate, ignoring the data actually given.

mcqs.stem: A graph of the volume of gas produced against time is steep at first and then gradually becomes horizontal. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is slow at the start and speeds up steadily
options.rationale: The rising line is read as a rising rate, because the total keeps getting bigger.

options.text: The reaction is fastest at the start, then slows and stops
options.rationale: The slope measures the rate, so a curve that flattens shows a rate that is falling to zero.

options.text: The reaction gets faster as the line on the graph flattens
options.rationale: Flat is read as fast, by analogy with a car on a level road rather than by reading the slope.

options.text: The reaction runs at a steady rate until the gas escapes
options.rationale: A steady rate would give a straight line, and this curve is not straight.

mcqs.stem: The line on a volume-of-gas graph becomes horizontal after 80 s. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The particles have run out of energy and can no longer react
options.rationale: Particles are pictured as tiring, which matches everyday experience but not the particle model.

options.text: The catalyst in the mixture has finally been used up as well
options.rationale: Assumes a catalyst is consumed, so that the reaction ends when the supply of it is exhausted.

options.text: One of the reactants has been completely used up by then
options.rationale: No more product can form once a reactant has run out, so the quantity collected stops changing.

options.text: The gas syringe has reached the end of its scale and stuck
options.rationale: An apparatus limit would truncate the graph, but it is not the chemical reason the reaction has finished.

mcqs.stem: A student needs the rate of reaction at 30 s from a curved graph of volume of gas against time. What should be drawn?

options.text: A straight line from the origin to the point at 30 s
options.rationale: Easier to draw because it joins two clear points, but its slope gives the mean rate up to 30 s.

options.text: A straight line joining the points at 0 s and at 60 s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see no difference between an average over a period and the rate at an instant.

options.text: A vertical line from 30 s up to the curve, then read off
options.rationale: This reads the quantity of gas collected at 30 s, which is a volume rather than a rate.

options.text: A tangent touching the curve at 30 s, then find its slope
options.rationale: The slope of a tangent drawn at that point is used as the measure of the rate of reaction there.

mcqs.stem: Tangents are drawn to the same curve at 10 s and at 50 s. The tangent at 10 s is the steeper of the two. What does this show?

options.text: The rate of reaction at 10 s is greater than the rate at 50 s
options.rationale: The slope of the tangent measures the rate at that time, so the steeper tangent marks the faster moment.

options.text: The rate of reaction at 50 s is greater than the rate at 10 s
options.rationale: Steepness is read as slowness, the reverse of the relationship between slope and rate.

options.text: The mean rate is the same at both of these times on the curve
options.rationale: Treats a reaction as having one single rate, so the two tangents are thought to tell you nothing new.

options.text: More gas had been collected at 10 s than had been at 50 s
options.rationale: Confuses the steepness of the curve with its height; the volume collected is still rising at 50 s.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A tangent drawn to the curve at 20 s passes through the points (10 s, 12 cm³) and (30 s, 48 cm³). What is the rate of reaction at 20 s?

options.text: 1.6 cm³/s
options.rationale: 48 / 30: one point's coordinates divided as though the line ran from the origin.

options.text: 1.8 cm³/s
options.rationale: Gradient = change in volume / change in time = (48 − 12) / (30 − 10) = 36 / 20 = 1.8 cm³/s.

options.text: 0.56 cm³/s
options.rationale: 20 / 36: the change in time divided by the change in volume.

options.text: 2.4 cm³/s
options.rationale: 48 / 20: the higher volume divided by the time the tangent was drawn at.

mcqs.stem: (HT) For the same reaction, the gradient of the tangent at 20 s is larger than the mean rate over the whole reaction. Why?

options.text: The gradient is always twice the value of the mean rate
options.rationale: Invents a fixed relationship; the factor depends entirely on the shape of the curve.

options.text: The gradient is measured in a different unit from the rate
options.rationale: Both are in cm³/s; the student assumes a difference in numbers must come from a difference in units.

options.text: The gradient gives the rate at that moment, not an average
options.rationale: The mean is pulled down by the slow later stages, while the tangent measures the rate at 20 s only.

options.text: The gradient is the total gas divided by the total time
options.rationale: This describes the mean rate, so it would give the same value rather than a larger one.

mcqs.stem: How does cooling a reaction mixture affect the rate of the reaction, and why?

options.text: It decreases the rate, but only because collisions are fewer
options.rationale: The frequency argument used for the other factors is applied to temperature and stopped there.

options.text: It increases the rate: the particles are packed more closely
options.rationale: Cooling does contract a mixture slightly, and the student treats crowding as the dominant effect.

options.text: It has no effect on the rate, only on the product formed
options.rationale: Rate and yield are confused, so a change in conditions is thought to alter the amount rather than the speed.

options.text: It decreases the rate: collisions are fewer and less energetic
options.rationale: Temperature affects both the frequency of collisions and their energy, so lowering it reduces the rate on both counts.

mcqs.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?

options.text: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
options.rationale: Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate.

options.text: Each acid particle is given more energy, so more collisions are successful
options.rationale: 'Stronger' acid is taken to mean more energetic particles rather than more crowded ones.

options.text: The acid particles move faster, so they collide with the metal much harder
options.rationale: Particle speed is imported from the temperature explanation, where it does belong.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra acid present
options.rationale: Activation energy becomes the catch-all explanation for anything that makes a reaction go faster.

mcqs.stem: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure of the gas mixture increase the rate of reaction?

options.text: Squeezing the gases makes the particles move faster and hit harder
options.rationale: Pressure is merged with temperature, helped by the everyday warmth of a bicycle pump.

options.text: The particles are closer together, so they collide more frequently
options.rationale: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.

options.text: The activation energy falls when the gases are pushed together
options.rationale: Any increase in rate is attributed to a lower energy barrier rather than to more frequent collisions.

options.text: Each collision now releases more energy, which speeds up the rest
options.rationale: Confuses the energy given out by the reaction with the energy needed for collisions to succeed.

mcqs.stem: A 5 g strip of magnesium and 5 g of magnesium powder are each added to excess acid. Why does the powder react faster?

options.text: The powder contains more magnesium than the strip does, so more of it reacts
options.rationale: The bulkier appearance of a powder suggests more material, although both samples are 5 g.

options.text: The powder grains are lighter, so they move faster and collide much harder
options.rationale: Particle motion, which belongs to gases and solutions, is transferred to grains of a solid.

options.text: The powder has a greater surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent
options.rationale: More of the magnesium is exposed to the acid, so acid particles collide with magnesium atoms more often.

options.text: The powder is more concentrated than the strip, so its particles are closer
options.rationale: Concentration applies to solutions; both samples are the same solid with the same density.

mcqs.stem: A cube of a solid reactant is cut into eight smaller cubes. What happens to the solid?

options.text: There is now more solid available to react than there was before
options.rationale: Smaller pieces spread further and look like more material, though nothing has been added.

options.text: Its surface area to volume ratio falls as the pieces get smaller
options.rationale: 'Smaller' is applied to the ratio itself without comparing the two quantities in it.

options.text: Its surface area is unchanged because it is still the same solid
options.rationale: Treats surface area as a fixed property of the substance rather than of its shape.

options.text: Its total surface area increases while its volume stays the same
options.rationale: Cutting exposes faces that were inside the cube, so the surface area to volume ratio rises.

mcqs.stem: According to collision theory, when can a chemical reaction between two particles occur?

options.text: Only when they collide with at least the activation energy
options.rationale: Reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

options.text: Whenever two of the reacting particles collide with each other
options.rationale: The frequency half of collision theory is remembered and the energy condition dropped.

options.text: When the particles take in the energy the reaction gives out
options.rationale: Confuses the barrier that must be reached with the energy released once the reaction happens.

options.text: When the particles have been thoroughly mixed in the flask
options.rationale: Mixing brings particles into contact but says nothing about the energy of the collisions.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: The energy that is given out by the reaction as it takes place
options.rationale: Both quantities appear on a reaction profile, and 'activation' sounds like a release of energy.

options.text: The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of activation energy.

options.text: The energy that is needed to make two particles collide at all
options.rationale: Ties the energy to the act of colliding rather than to the barrier the collision must clear.

options.text: The average energy that every particle in the mixture will have
options.rationale: Describes the energy particles happen to have, not the minimum they need.

mcqs.stem: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction? Give the full explanation.

options.text: Collisions become more frequent, and that is the whole explanation
options.rationale: The frequency sentence learned for concentration and pressure is reused and left incomplete.

options.text: Collisions become more energetic but they are no more frequent
options.rationale: Temperature is filed as 'the energy factor', so its effect on frequency is denied.

options.text: Collisions become more frequent and more of them have enough energy
options.rationale: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction falls as the mixture heats
options.rationale: Lowering the barrier is offered for any faster reaction, but only a catalyst does that.

mcqs.stem: The rate of a reaction is 0.4 cm³/s using 0.5 mol/dm³ acid. Using simple ideas about proportionality, what rate is predicted with 1.0 mol/dm³ acid?

options.text: 0.2 cm³/s
options.rationale: The relationship is inverted, as though a stronger solution made the reaction take longer.

options.text: 0.4 cm³/s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a change in concentration alters the amount of gas rather than the rate.

options.text: 1.6 cm³/s
options.rationale: The doubling is applied twice, giving four times the original rate.

options.text: 0.8 cm³/s
options.rationale: Doubling the concentration doubles the frequency of collisions, so the rate is predicted to double.

mcqs.stem: Doubling the concentration of a solution roughly doubles the rate of reaction. Which explanation uses collision theory correctly?

options.text: Twice as many particles in the same volume give twice the collision frequency
options.rationale: This is the simple proportional argument the specification asks for: crowding doubles, so collisions double.

options.text: Twice the concentration gives each particle twice as much energy to react with
options.rationale: Concentration is treated as an energy factor rather than a crowding factor.

options.text: Twice the concentration halves the activation energy the reaction needs
options.rationale: A lower barrier is offered as the reason, but only a catalyst provides a lower-energy pathway.

options.text: Twice the concentration makes twice as much product form in the reaction
options.rationale: Answers a question about yield instead of one about rate.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 5, one method follows the reaction by measuring the volume of gas produced. Which measurements are taken?

options.text: The total volume of gas collected once bubbling stops
options.rationale: A single final volume gives the amount of product but no information about how fast it formed.

options.text: The volume in the gas syringe at fixed time intervals
options.rationale: Readings taken at set times give the quantity of product formed over time, from which the rate is found.

options.text: The time from the start until the first bubble appears
options.rationale: A time on its own is offered as the rate, and this one measures only how quickly the reaction started.

options.text: The volume of acid left in the flask at the very end
options.rationale: Plausible as a measure of reactant used, but it cannot be measured accurately and is not taken over time.

mcqs.stem: In the sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid method, the mixture turns cloudy and a cross under the flask disappears. What does a shorter time show?

options.text: A slower reaction, because there was less time for it to react
options.rationale: The stopwatch reading is read directly as the rate, so a small number looks like a small rate.

options.text: A faster reaction, because more sulfur was made altogether
options.rationale: The right conclusion for the wrong reason: the amount of sulfur is the same, it just forms sooner.

options.text: A faster reaction, because the sulfur was formed more quickly
options.rationale: The same degree of cloudiness is reached sooner, so the reaction producing the sulfur is faster.

options.text: No change in rate, because the same mass of sulfur is formed
options.rationale: Quantity is used in place of rate, so equal quantities are taken to mean equal rates.

mcqs.stem: Required practical 5 involves developing a hypothesis. Which of these is a suitable hypothesis for the investigation?

options.text: The cross took less time to disappear with the concentrated solution
options.rationale: This is a result, written in the past tense after the experiment rather than before it.

options.text: The concentration will be changed and the temperature kept the same
options.rationale: Identifies the independent and control variables, which is part of the method, not the hypothesis.

options.text: The rate of the reaction depends on how the experiment is carried out
options.rationale: Too vague to test: it names no variable and offers no scientific reason.

options.text: A higher concentration gives more frequent collisions, so a greater rate
options.rationale: A testable idea proposed in advance that states the expected relationship and the reasoning behind it.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about catalysts is correct?

options.text: They change the rate of a reaction but are not used up in it
options.rationale: This is the specification's statement: catalysts change the rate but are not used up during the reaction.

options.text: They are used up slowly and have to be replaced now and then
options.rationale: Anything added to a flask is assumed to be consumed by the reaction it affects.

options.text: They increase the amount of product that a reaction can make
options.rationale: Rate and yield are confused, so a faster reaction is thought to be a more productive one.

options.text: They will speed up any reaction that they are added to
options.rationale: The memorised definition mentions no link to a particular reaction, so generality is assumed.

mcqs.stem: What is the role of enzymes in living things?

options.text: They are living substances that get used up as they work
options.rationale: Enzymes are filed under biology rather than chemistry, so the catalyst definition is not applied.

options.text: They act as catalysts for reactions in biological systems
options.rationale: The specification states that enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.

options.text: They supply the energy that biological reactions need
options.rationale: Catalysts are pictured as giving particles energy rather than lowering the barrier.

options.text: They are catalysts that work in any reaction in the body
options.rationale: Half right: enzymes are catalysts, but different reactions need different ones.

mcqs.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: It gives the reacting particles extra energy so that more can react
options.rationale: If more collisions now succeed, students assume the particles must have been given more energy.

options.text: It lowers the energy of the products so more energy is given out
options.rationale: 'Lower activation energy' is remembered as simply 'lower', so the whole profile is dropped.

options.text: It provides a different pathway that has a lower activation energy
options.rationale: With a lower barrier, a greater proportion of the collisions already have sufficient energy to react.

options.text: It makes the particles collide with one another far more often
options.rationale: Frequency is the mechanism for concentration, pressure and surface area, not for a catalyst.

mcqs.stem: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, how does the catalysed curve differ from the uncatalysed one?

options.text: It has a lower peak and a lower level for the products formed
options.rationale: The catalysed curve is remembered as 'the lower one' and is drawn lower all the way along.

options.text: It starts at a higher reactant level, so less energy is needed
options.rationale: The catalyst is pictured as giving the reactants a boost up towards the barrier.

options.text: It has the same peak but reaches the products in a shorter time
options.rationale: The horizontal axis is read as time, so a faster reaction is expected to give a narrower curve.

options.text: It has a lower peak, but the same reactant and product levels
options.rationale: Only the activation energy changes, so the two curves begin and end at the same energies.

mcqs.stem: Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes slowly. When manganese(IV) oxide is added it decomposes rapidly, and the manganese(IV) oxide is recovered unchanged. What does this show?

options.text: It is a catalyst: it changes the rate and is not used up
options.rationale: Both pieces of evidence the specification asks students to use are present: an effect on rate, and no net consumption.

options.text: It is a reactant, so it belongs in the equation for this reaction
options.rationale: Everything placed in the flask is assumed to belong on the left of the arrow.

options.text: It is a catalyst, so it will speed up other reactions too
options.rationale: The identification is right but the generalisation is not: different reactions need different catalysts.

options.text: It is a product, because it is there at the end of the reaction
options.rationale: Being present at the end is taken as proof it was made, ignoring that it was there at the start.

mcqs.stem: The equation for a reaction is 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. A solid added to the hydrogen peroxide makes it decompose much faster and is still there at the end. How can you tell the solid is a catalyst?

options.text: It appears on the left of the equation as one of the reactants
options.rationale: The equation is built from what is added to the flask rather than from what is chemically changed.

options.text: It changes the rate but does not appear in the chemical equation
options.rationale: Catalysts are identified from their effect on the rate and because they are not included in the equation.

options.text: It is used up in the reaction, which is why it speeds things up
options.rationale: Contradicts the evidence in the stem, but matches the belief that a catalyst is consumed.

options.text: It increases the mass of oxygen that this reaction produces
options.rationale: The oxygen is fixed by the hydrogen peroxide present; the catalyst changes only how quickly it forms.

mcqs.stem: 0.10 g of magnesium reacts with excess 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. The experiment is repeated with 2.0 mol/dm³ acid and the same mass of magnesium. What happens?

options.text: The gas is given off faster, and the final volume is doubled
options.rationale: Doubling the concentration is assumed to double everything, including the yield.

options.text: The gas comes off at the same rate, as the metal is unchanged
options.rationale: The limiting reactant is thought to control the speed as well as the amount.

options.text: The gas is given off faster, and the final volume is the same
options.rationale: The magnesium is the reactant used up, so it fixes the total gas; the higher concentration only raises the rate.

options.text: The gas is given off faster, and the final volume is smaller
options.rationale: A fast reaction is imagined to waste some of the magnesium, leaving less gas.
